title: Chinese AI tool pulled to prevent 'misuse' after South Korea hacks
key_facts: The developer of the Chinese AI cybersecurity tool Artex, known as "Autumn-27", said on Thursday 8 Oct 2026 on GitHub that the project would no longer be updated and would become closed-source.
South Korea's government said that week it was "highly likely" Artex was used in breaches at more than seven financial institutions.
South Korea's Financial Services Commission said more than 68,000 people were affected; Shinhan Bank said loan-application data of about 25,000 customers leaked (names, phone numbers, annual income).
CrowdStrike said its investigation suggested the attacker used Artex and was potentially a 26-year-old based in China, likely a Chinese speaker and financially motivated.
In Japan about 20 companies reported possible data compromises in similar attacks; police said it was unclear whether the cases were connected.
Experts said closing the code may make it harder for new users to obtain but does not remove copies already downloaded.
quote_evidence: Experts said making Artex closed-source could make it harder for new users to obtain and adapt, but would not remove copies already downloaded.
Police chief Yoshinobu Kusunoki said it remained unclear whether the cases were connected.
South Korea's Financial Services Commission said more than 68,000 people had been affected by the hacks.
why_it_matters_hint: A defensive tool turned into an attack tool is being locked down after bank breaches, but copies remain in circulation.
